questions.question: How does the signer check a signature when several secret keys are configured?
questions.reference: Signer.verify_signature base64-decodes the signature, then tries each secret key from newest to oldest (reversed secret_keys), derives a key from it and returns True on the first key whose algorithm signature matches; otherwise False.

questions.question: When I pass a list of secret keys, which one is used to create new signatures?
questions.reference: The newest key, which is the last item of the secret_keys list. Older keys are only kept so existing signatures can still be verified.

questions.question: What key derivation methods are supported and which one is the default?
questions.reference: concat, django-concat, hmac and none. The default is django-concat, which hashes salt + b'signer' + secret key. An unknown method raises TypeError.

questions.question: Which hash function is used by default for signing?
questions.reference: SHA-1, through the _lazy_sha1 helper used as default_digest_method, combined with HMAC.

questions.question: Why is hashlib.sha1 only accessed at runtime instead of at import?
questions.reference: FIPS builds of Python may not include SHA-1, so using it eagerly as a default would fail at import before the developer can configure a different digest method.

questions.question: How is the signature comparison protected against timing attacks?
questions.reference: SigningAlgorithm.verify_signature compares the expected and given signatures with hmac.compare_digest, a constant-time comparison.

questions.question: What happens if I choose a separator character that could appear in base64?
questions.reference: The Signer constructor raises ValueError, because ASCII letters, digits and '-_=' can appear in the signature itself.

questions.question: What does NoneAlgorithm do?
questions.reference: It performs no signing: get_signature always returns an empty byte string.

questions.question: What error do I get when unsigning a value that has no separator in it?
questions.reference: Signer.unsign raises BadSignature saying no separator was found. If the separator is present but the signature does not match it raises BadSignature with the payload attached.

questions.question: How is the timestamp stored inside a value signed by TimestampSigner?
questions.reference: The current integer timestamp is converted to bytes and base64 encoded, appended to the value with the separator, and the signature is computed over value + sep + timestamp and appended after another separator.

questions.question: Which exception is raised when a signed token is older than max_age?
questions.reference: SignatureExpired, a subclass of BadTimeSignature, with a message comparing the age to max_age and date_signed set to when the value was signed.

questions.question: What happens if a token's timestamp is in the future?
questions.reference: If max_age is given and the computed age is negative, unsign raises SignatureExpired with a message that the age is less than 0 seconds.

questions.question: How can I find out when a value was signed?
questions.reference: Call unsign (or loads on a timed serializer) with return_timestamp=True; it returns the value together with a timezone-aware UTC datetime produced by timestamp_to_datetime.

questions.question: How does the URL safe serializer keep tokens short?
questions.reference: dump_payload zlib-compresses the JSON and keeps the compressed form only if it is shorter, then base64 encodes it and prefixes a '.' to mark it as compressed.

questions.question: How does loading know whether a URL safe payload was compressed?
questions.reference: If the payload starts with '.', load_payload strips it and zlib-decompresses after base64 decoding; failures raise BadPayload.

questions.question: What are fallback_signers used for in a Serializer?
questions.reference: They are extra signer configurations tried when unsigning, for example an older digest method. iter_unsigners yields the main signer first, then each fallback (a kwargs dict, a Signer class, or a (class, kwargs) tuple) for every secret key.

questions.question: How does Serializer.loads behave when the first signer fails?
questions.reference: It tries every signer from iter_unsigners in turn, returning the first successful load_payload result, and if all fail it re-raises the last BadSignature.

questions.question: What does loads_unsafe return and when should I use it?
questions.reference: It returns a (signature_valid, payload) tuple and still loads the payload when the signature is bad. It is meant for debugging only, with a serializer that is not exploitable.

questions.question: Which exception is raised when a payload can't be deserialized?
questions.reference: BadPayload, a subclass of BadData, which can carry the original_error that caused decoding to fail.

questions.question: What is the hierarchy of the exceptions this library defines?
questions.reference: BadData is the base. BadSignature and BadPayload subclass it; BadTimeSignature and BadHeader subclass BadSignature; SignatureExpired subclasses BadTimeSignature.

questions.question: Does the expired-signature error tell me when the token was originally created?
questions.reference: Yes. BadTimeSignature (and so SignatureExpired) has a date_signed attribute with the timezone-aware datetime when the value was signed, useful for telling users how stale a link is.

questions.question: How does the library handle base64 padding?
questions.reference: base64_encode uses URL-safe base64 and strips trailing '=' padding; base64_decode adds the padding back before decoding and raises BadData on invalid input.

questions.question: How are integer timestamps turned into bytes?
questions.reference: With a big-endian unsigned 64-bit struct ('>Q'); int_to_bytes packs and strips leading zero bytes, bytes_to_int left-pads to 8 bytes and unpacks.

questions.question: Why should different parts of an app use different salts?
questions.reference: The salt is combined with the secret key to derive a unique key per context, so a token made for one purpose (for example an activation link) cannot be loaded by a serializer meant for another purpose.

questions.question: How should I generate and store the secret key?
questions.reference: Use a long random string of bytes, for example from os.urandom, keep it secret, and load it from outside the code such as an environment variable rather than committing it.

questions.question: What salt is used by default if I don't pass one?
questions.reference: Signer defaults to b'itsdangerous.Signer' (also used when salt=None), while Serializer defaults to b'itsdangerous'.
